caption: D latch, 4 blocks: the data input feeds a repeater (on a stone) whose output is q, and the enable input feeds a second repeater pointing into its side. While that second repeater is on, the first is locked and holds q; while it is off, q follows d. So it is transparent while e is OFF; for a latch that follows d while e is ON, hang the 1-block NOT (a wall torch) on the enable input and let it feed the side repeater (5 blocks). Latency 4 ticks.

Counter 3, dropper corner ring, 8 blocks (track memory): the input cell touches three droppers on three axes (east, up, south); between each pair a hopper carries the stone on to the next dropper (dropper up -> hopper west -> dropper south -> hopper down -> dropper east -> hopper north). Each pulse fires all three; only the one holding the stone moves it, and its hopper delivers it after all three have fired, so the stone advances one dropper per pulse whatever the firing order. The comparator reads the east dropper: on during one pulse window in three (level style).

Counter 2 as a divider, two copper bulbs, 6 blocks (track memory): the input toggles bulb 1, its comparator toggles bulb 2 on every second pulse; bulb 2's comparator changes state once every two pulses and holds between (toggles style). The same build is counter4-bulb2, which is how the bulb chain is tuned: this entry is its divider reading, not a second machine, and a counter 2 needs only the 3-block counter2-bulb.

Counter 4, two copper bulbs, 6 blocks (track memory): the input toggles bulb 1, its comparator toggles bulb 2 on every second pulse, and bulb 2's comparator is the output: on for two pulse windows, off for two (level style, period 4; the same build divides by 2 as a toggle stream).

Counter 8, three copper bulbs, 9 blocks (track memory): a chain of three bulb T flip-flops (bulb + comparator each), each comparator toggling the next bulb; the last comparator is on for four pulse windows and off for four (level style, period 8).

Counter 6, dropper corner ring + copper bulb, 11 blocks (track memory): the counter3-corner ring (the input cell touches three droppers; hoppers pass the stone one dropper per pulse) lights its comparator one window in three; that comparator toggles a copper bulb, read by a second comparator: on for three pulse windows, off for three (level style, period 6; as a toggle stream it divides by 3). D flip-flop, 9 blocks: the data runs through two repeaters, and each has a lock repeater beside it (a locked repeater holds its output). The master's lock reads the clock block itself, so the first repeater follows d only while the clock is LOW; a wall torch hanging on that same clock block feeds the slave's lock, so the second repeater passes only while the clock is HIGH. On the rising edge the master freezes on d and the slave opens: q takes d exactly at the edge. No clock wiring at all: the clock block is part of the circuit.

D flip-flop with enable, 12 blocks: the 9-block flip-flop (two repeaters with lock repeaters beside them; the master's lock reads the clock block, a wall torch on that block feeds the slave's) plus one more lock on the slave's other side, fed by a wall torch on the enable block. A repeater is locked if EITHER side is powered, so while e is off the slave stays locked through any clock edge and q holds; no AND gate is needed.

2-bit shift register, 27 blocks: two repeater-lock flip-flops in a row, the first stage's output feeding the second stage's data. The first stage reads the clock block directly (its master lock behind it, its slave's wall torch hanging on it); a dust on top of the clock block carries the clock round to the second stage's stone, which plays the same part for it. On each rising edge both stages shift at once.

Counter 100, 23 blocks, with items (track memory, `mctas circuit memory items --n 100`): the output toggles once every 100 pulses, and the same 23 blocks count any N up to 576; only the number of items loaded changes. Two droppers face each other and hold 100 items between them; each pulse fires only one of them, so the pile walks from one to the other and each runs empty once every 100 pulses. A comparator reads each dropper, and the torch on its output block is lit exactly while that dropper is empty; both torches touch the copper bulb, which therefore toggles each time a dropper runs empty. The bulb is the phase: a comparator reading it powers the stone under the left dropper, which holds it (a dropper kept powered sees no new pulse), and through a dust under the right dropper switches off the torch beside it, which held the right one. The pulse reaches the right dropper through the input block on its lid and the left one through a dust on its own lid.

The bulb is the phase: a comparator reading it powers the stone under the left dropper, which holds it (a dropper kept powered sees no new pulse), and through a dust under the right dropper switches off the torch beside it, which held the right one. The pulse reaches the right dropper through the input block on its lid and the left one through a dust on its own lid.

T flip-flop with reset, 7 blocks: two droppers and two hoppers in a ring pass one stone around, and a comparator reading the second dropper is the output. A t pulse fires both droppers; only the one holding the stone moves it, into a hopper that hands it on 8 ticks later, after both droppers have fired, so q toggles. One dust on the first hopper, under the t input block, fires both droppers at once: it points into the cells above them, and a dropper also fires on power in the cell above it. An r pulse fires the second dropper alone: if it holds the stone, the stone leaves and q clears; otherwise nothing moves.
